# Chapter: Native LINQ & F# Query Computation Expressions
*Source: articles/linq.md*

# LINQ Provider (`IQueryable`) & F# Query CE

Polars.NET contains a production-grade LINQ expression-tree compiler (`Polars.NET.Linq`) that translates standard C# `IQueryable<T>` queries and F# `query { }` computation expressions directly into native Rust `LazyFrame` physical plans. 

When a query is fully pushed down, Polars executes multithreaded SIMD kernels in Rust and directly yields a `DataFrame` **without allocating a single intermediate .NET row object**.

<div class="pl-pipeline">
  <div class="pl-pipeline-row">
    <div class="pl-step">
      <div class="pl-step-title">1. .NET Query Frontends</div>
      <div class="pl-step-desc">
        • C# LINQ Query Syntax (<code>from ... select ...</code>)<br>
        • C# Method Syntax (<code>.Where().Select()</code>)<br>
        • F# Query CE (<code>query { for ... select ... }</code>)
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="pl-arrow">→</div>
    <div class="pl-step">
      <div class="pl-step-title">2. Expression Tree Compiler</div>
      <div class="pl-step-desc">
        • <b>Tier 1</b>: 100% Native Pushdown (Rust DAG)<br>
        • <b>Tier 2</b>: Hybrid (Native Pushdown + Arrow Cursor)<br>
        • <b>Tier 3</b>: Strict Policy / Client Evaluation
      </div>
    </div>
    <div class="pl-arrow">→</div>
    <div class="pl-step">
      <div class="pl-step-title">3. Execution & Materialization</div>
      <div class="pl-step-desc">
        • <code>.ToDataFrame()</code>: Zero managed heap allocations<br>
        • <code>.ToLazyFrame()</code>: Escape to raw Polars DSL<br>
        • <code>.ToList() / .ToArray()</code>: Typed object hydration
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

---

## 1. Entrypoints & Query Materialization

To query a DataFrame or LazyFrame with LINQ, call `.AsQueryable<T>()`. The query executes lazily—no computation occurs until a terminal method is called:


```csharp [C# (Query Syntax)]
using Polars.CSharp;
using Polars.CSharp.Linq;

public record OrderDto(int OrderId, string Customer, string Region, double Revenue);

// 1. Enter LINQ from DataFrame or LazyFrame:
var query = from o in df.AsQueryable<OrderDto>()
            where o.Revenue >= 500.0 && o.Region != "Test"
            group o by o.Region into g
            select new {
                Region = g.Key,
                TotalRevenue = g.Sum(x => x.Revenue),
                OrderCount = g.Count()
            };

// 2. Materialize directly into a Polars DataFrame (Zero .NET Object Allocation):
using DataFrame resultDf = query.ToDataFrame();

// 3. Or inspect the compiled native plan:
Console.WriteLine(query.Explain());
```

```csharp [C# (Method Syntax)]
using Polars.CSharp;
using Polars.CSharp.Linq;

public record OrderDto(int OrderId, string Customer, string Region, double Revenue);

var query = df.AsQueryable<OrderDto>()
    .Where(o => o.Revenue >= 500.0 && o.Region != "Test")
    .GroupBy(o => o.Region)
    .Select(g => new {
        Region = g.Key,
        TotalRevenue = g.Sum(x => x.Revenue),
        OrderCount = g.Count()
    });

using DataFrame resultDf = query.ToDataFrame();
```

```fsharp [F# (Query CE)]
open System.Linq
open Polars.FSharp
open Polars.FSharp.Query

[<CLIMutable>]
type OrderDto = {
    OrderId: int
    Customer: string
    Region: string
    Revenue: float
}

// 1. Enter F# query { } computation expression:
let q =
    query {
        for o in df.AsQueryable<OrderDto>() do
        where (o.Revenue >= 500.0 && o.Region <> "Test")
        groupValBy o o.Region into g
        select {|
            Region = g.Key
            TotalRevenue = g.Sum(fun x -> x.Revenue)
            OrderCount = g.Count()
        |}
    }

// 2. Materialize to DataFrame:
use resultDf = q.ToDataFrame()

// 3. Or inspect the compiled native plan:
printfn "%s" (q.Explain())
```

```fsharp [F# (Pipeline API)]
open Polars.FSharp
open Polars.FSharp.Query

// Idiomatic F# pipeline combinators over Query
let resultDf =
    df.AsQueryable<OrderDto>()
    |> Query.where (fun o -> o.Revenue >= 500.0 && o.Region <> "Test")
    |> Query.toDataFrame
```


### Real Engine Plan & Output

Here is the exact logical execution plan and materialized DataFrame produced by Polars for the query above:

#### A. 100% Native Pushdown Plan (`query.Explain()`)


#### B. Materialized Native Output (`query.ToDataFrame()`)

### Direct Pipeline Entrypoints: Collections & ADO.NET Streams

Instead of manually creating a `DataFrame` or `LazyFrame` first, you can enter the Polars LINQ pipeline directly from in-memory collections or database streams using `AsPolarsQueryable`:

#### 1. In-Memory Collections (`IEnumerable<T>.AsPolarsQueryable()`)
Directly transposes any `List<T>`, array, or in-memory sequence into a native Polars LazyFrame and exposes it as a Polars LINQ queryable:

```csharp
using Polars.CSharp;
using Polars.CSharp.Linq;

List<OrderDto> orders = GetOrders();

// Ingest in-memory list straight into native Polars Rust execution:
using DataFrame topOrders = orders.AsPolarsQueryable()
    .Where(o => o.Revenue >= 500.0)
    .OrderByDescending(o => o.Revenue)
    .Take(100)
    .ToDataFrame();
```

#### 2. ADO.NET Database Streams (`IDataReader.AsPolarsQueryable()`)
Streams an open `IDataReader` directly into a Polars LINQ query with configurable batch size, bypassing intermediate object allocations:

```csharp
using System.Data;
using Microsoft.Data.SqlClient;
using Polars.CSharp;
using Polars.CSharp.Linq;

using var cmd = connection.CreateCommand();
cmd.CommandText = "SELECT OrderId, Customer, Region, Revenue FROM Orders";
using IDataReader reader = cmd.ExecuteReader();

// Streams database rows straight into Polars LINQ engine:
using DataFrame regionalSales = reader.AsPolarsQueryable<OrderDto>(batchSize: 50_000)
    .Where(o => o.Revenue > 100.0)
    .GroupBy(o => o.Region)
    .Select(g => new {
        Region = g.Key,
        TotalRevenue = g.Sum(x => x.Revenue),
        OrderCount = g.Count()
    })
    .ToDataFrame();
```

#### 3. Seamless In-Memory Collection Interop (Join, Concat & Union)

The Polars LINQ provider seamlessly accepts arbitrary in-memory .NET collections (`List<T>`, arrays, `IEnumerable<T>`) as operands inside active queries without manual pre-conversion:

* **In-Memory Join Pushdown**: Join a Polars DataFrame query directly with an in-memory lookup collection (`List<TInner>`). The provider transposes the in-memory sequence into native Arrow batches and executes a Tier-1 100% native pushdown join in Rust:
  ```csharp
  var inMemoryCustomers = new List<Customer>
  {
      new(1, "Alice"),
      new(2, "Bob")
  };

  // query is a Polars queryable over a high-volume DataFrame or LazyFrame:
  var enrichedQuery = ordersQuery.Join(
      inMemoryCustomers, // Arbitrary in-memory List<T>
      o => o.CustomerId,
      c => c.Id,
      (o, c) => new { o.OrderId, c.Name, o.Amount }
  );

  using DataFrame resultDf = enrichedQuery.ToDataFrame();
  ```

* **In-Memory Concat & Union Pushdown**: Append or merge in-memory rows directly into a Polars query:
  ```csharp
  var extraEmployees = new List<Employee>
  {
      new("Charlie", 35, 70000),
      new("David", 40, 80000)
  };

  // Concatenate in-memory collection straight into the native physical plan:
  var combinedQuery = query.Where(e => e.Age >= 25).Concat(extraEmployees);
  using DataFrame combinedDf = combinedQuery.ToDataFrame();
  ```

> [!NOTE] Native Transposition Guarantee
> When an in-memory collection participates in a `Join`, `Concat`, `Union`, or `Merge` operation, Polars.NET automatically transposes the managed objects into Arrow contiguous arrays, pushes execution into native Rust SIMD kernels, and preserves full query optimization.

---

## 2. Terminal Methods: What Can You Materialize?

Polars.NET LINQ queries support diverse terminal materialization pathways depending on your scenario:

| Method | Target | Performance Characteristics |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`.ToDataFrame()`** / **`.ToDataFrameAsync()`** | `DataFrame` | **Fastest**. 100% native Rust execution; zero .NET object hydration. |
| **`.ToLazyFrame()`** | `LazyFrame` | Compiles the LINQ pipeline to a native `LazyFrame` for continued raw Polars DSL chaining. |
| **`.ToSeries(name)`** | `Series` | Extracts a single column or composite struct series from a projected query. |
| **`.ToList()`** / **`.ToArray()`** | `List<T>` / `T[]` | Materializes typed .NET objects via pre-compiled stack cursors. |
| **`await foreach`** / **`.ToAsyncEnumerable()`** | `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` | Asynchronous non-blocking streaming without thread starvation. |
| **`.First()`** / **`.Single()`** / **`.Count()`** | Scalar | Scalar aggregations pushed down to single-row reduction kernels. |

---

## 3. Supported Native BCL & C# Method Mappings

The LINQ provider automatically translates standard .NET Base Class Library (BCL) calls into vectorized Polars expressions:

<div class="pl-pipeline">
  <div class="pl-pipeline-row">
    <div class="pl-step">
      <div class="pl-step-title">C# BCL Expressions</div>
      <div class="pl-step-desc"><code>s.Name.ToUpper()</code><br><code>s.Created.Year</code><br><code>Math.Round(s.Price, 2)</code><br><code>Regex.IsMatch(s.Email, pattern)</code></div>
    </div>
    <div class="pl-arrow">→ <i>Compiled to</i> →</div>
    <div class="pl-step">
      <div class="pl-step-title">Rust Vectorized Kernels</div>
      <div class="pl-step-desc"><code>col("Name").str.to_uppercase()</code><br><code>col("Created").dt.year()</code><br><code>col("Price").round(2)</code><br><code>col("Email").str.contains(pattern)</code></div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

| Category | Supported .NET Operations | Compiled Native Polars Expression |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Strings** | `s.Contains(x)`, `s.StartsWith(x)`, `s.EndsWith(x)`, `s.ToUpper()`, `s.ToLower()`, `s.Trim()`, `s.Substring(start, len)`, `s.Replace(a, b)`, `s.Length`, `string.IsNullOrEmpty(s)` | `.Str.Contains()`, `.Str.StartsWith()`, `.Str.ToUppercase()`, `.Str.Slice()`, `.Str.ReplaceAll()`, `.Str.LenBytes()` |
| **Mathematics** | `Math.Abs(x)`, `Math.Round(x, n)`, `Math.Floor(x)`, `Math.Ceiling(x)`, `Math.Sqrt(x)`, `Math.Pow(x, y)`, `Math.Log(x)`, `Math.Exp(x)`, `Math.Sin(x)`, `Math.Clamp(x, min, max)` | `.Abs()`, `.Round()`, `.Floor()`, `.Ceil()`, `.Sqrt()`, `.Pow()`, `.Log()`, `.Exp()`, `.Sin()`, `.Clip()` |
| **Date & Time** | `dt.Year`, `dt.Month`, `dt.Day`, `dt.Hour`, `dt.Minute`, `dt.Second`, `dt.DayOfWeek`, `dt.DayOfYear`, `dt.Date`, `dt.AddDays(n)` | `.Dt.Year()`, `.Dt.Month()`, `.Dt.Day()`, `.Dt.Hour()`, `.Dt.Minute()`, `.Dt.Second()`, `.Dt.Weekday()`, `.Dt.OffsetBy()` |
| **Regular Expressions** | `Regex.IsMatch(s, pattern)` | `.Str.Contains(pattern)` using native Rust high-performance regex engine |
| **Collections & Lists** | `item.Tags.Contains("promo")`, `item.Tags.Length`, `items.SelectMany(x => x.Tags)` | `.List.Contains()`, `.List.Len()`, Native **`.Explode()`** |
| **Conditionals** | `x ? a : b`, `a ?? b` | Native ternary `When.Then.Otherwise` and `Coalesce` kernels |

---

## 4. The 3-Tier Execution Architecture

When you call `query.Explain()`, Polars.NET reports one of three execution tiers:

### Tier 1: `[100% Native Pushdown]`
Every filtering, sorting, grouping, joining, and projection stage is translated into native Polars Rust expressions.
* **Heap Impact**: Zero managed heap allocations during execution.
* **Throughput**: Maximum SIMD vectorized throughput.

### Tier 2: `[Hybrid Execution (Partial Pushdown)]`
Filtering, sorting, and grouping run 100% in Rust. Only custom user code in the final `.Select(...)` (such as formatting or calling external helper functions) is evaluated on the client via a fast struct cursor:

```csharp
var query = df.AsQueryable<Transaction>()
    .Where(t => t.Amount > 100)                      // Native Pushdown (Rust)
    .OrderByDescending(t => t.Amount)               // Native Pushdown (Rust)
    .Select(t => new {                              // Client Evaluation on final row:
        t.Id,
        FormattedDisplay = FormatExternal(t.Amount) // Custom C# method
    });
```

### Tier 3: Client Evaluation Policy & `PolarsPushdownException`
By default, Polars.NET adopts a **Strict Policy** (`ClientEvaluationPolicy.Strict`). If an unsupported custom method is used inside an *intermediate* stage (`Where`, `GroupBy`, `Join`), the provider throws `PolarsPushdownException` to prevent silent performance degradation:

```csharp
// [Error] Throws PolarsPushdownException: CustomMethod cannot be evaluated inside Rust SIMD kernel!
var query = df.AsQueryable<Item>().Where(x => MyCustomHelper(x.Score));
```

#### How to Address Pushdown Exceptions:
1. **Best Practice**: Replace custom methods with supported BCL functions (`string`, `Math`, `Regex`).
2. **Hybrid Projection**: Move custom formatting into the terminal `.Select(...)` clause.
3. **Explicit Client Evaluation**: Call `.AsEnumerable()` (C#) or `.AsSeq()` (F#) to consciously switch to in-memory LINQ:
   ```csharp
   // Explicitly offload to client:
   var result = df.AsQueryable<Item>()
       .Where(x => x.Active)               // Pushed down to Polars
       .AsEnumerable()                     // Explicit client barrier
       .Where(x => MyCustomHelper(x.Score)); // Evaluated on client
   ```

---

## 5. Extended Analytics Operators in LINQ

Standard C# LINQ syntax lacks window functions, lag/lead operators, and time-series tools. `Polars.CSharp.Linq` fills this gap by introducing extension methods usable directly inside LINQ `.Select(...)`:


```csharp [C# (Window Functions & Shifts)]
using Polars.CSharp.Linq;

var query = df.AsQueryable<Employee>()
    .Select(e => new
    {
        e.Name,
        e.DepartmentId,
        e.Salary,
        // 1. Window Function: Group Average
        DeptAvg = e.Salary.Average().Over(e.DepartmentId),
        
        // 2. Window Deviation
        DiffFromAvg = e.Salary - e.Salary.Average().Over(e.DepartmentId),
        
        // 3. Dense Ranking within department
        DeptRank = e.Salary.Rank(RankMethod.Dense, descending: true).Over(e.DepartmentId),
        
        // 4. Time-series Lead / Lag Shift
        PrevSalary = e.Salary.Shift(1).Over(e.DepartmentId)
    });
```

```csharp [C# (Time-Series Interpolation)]
using Polars.CSharp.Linq;

var cleanQuery = df.AsQueryable<SensorReading>()
    .Select(r => new
    {
        r.Timestamp,
        r.DeviceId,
        // Linear interpolation over missing sensor readings partitioned by Device
        CleanVal = r.RawValue.Interpolate(InterpolationMethod.Linear).Over(r.DeviceId)
    });
```


---

## 6. The Bidirectional Escape Hatch

No matter how capable a LINQ provider is, advanced analytics occasionally require specialized engine-specific features (such as regex unnesting, Parquet scan tuning, or Aho-Corasick matching). Polars.NET provides a seamless **Bidirectional Escape Hatch**:

<div class="pl-pipeline">
  <div class="pl-pipeline-row">
    <div class="pl-step" style="text-align: center;">
      <div class="pl-step-title">IQueryable&lt;T&gt; (LINQ Provider)</div>
      <div class="pl-step-desc">Typed C# queries and F# <code>query { }</code> with BCL expressions</div>
    </div>
    <div class="pl-arrow">⇄ <code>query.ToLazyFrame()</code> / <code>lf.AsQueryable&lt;T&gt;()</code> ⇄</div>
    <div class="pl-step" style="text-align: center;">
      <div class="pl-step-title">LazyFrame (Native Polars DSL)</div>
      <div class="pl-step-desc">Raw Rust SIMD kernels, Selectors, and Streaming engine</div>
    </div>
  </div>
</div>

### Pattern 1: LINQ to Native LazyFrame (`.ToLazyFrame()`)
Start with familiar LINQ for relational filtering and joining, then seamlessly switch to native Polars DSL for specialized operations:

```csharp
// 1. Build initial filtering using comfortable LINQ:
var baseQuery = df.AsQueryable<LogEntry>()
    .Where(e => e.Level == "ERROR" && e.Timestamp >= DateTime.UtcNow.AddDays(-7));

// 2. Escape hatch to native LazyFrame:
using LazyFrame lf = baseQuery.ToLazyFrame();

// 3. Apply raw Polars domain operations (Regex extraction, etc.):
using DataFrame finalDf = lf
    .WithColumns(Pl.Col("Message").Str.ExtractAll(@"\[code:(\d+)\]").Alias("ErrorCodes"))
    .Collect();
```

### Pattern 2: Native LazyFrame to LINQ (`.AsQueryable<T>()`)
Conversely, start with specialized file scanning or partition pruning, and switch back to LINQ:

```csharp
// 1. Scan with specialized low-level parquet tuning:
using LazyFrame lf = LazyFrame.ScanParquet("telemetry/*.parquet")
    .Filter(Pl.Col("DeviceType") == "IoT");

// 2. Resume querying with standard LINQ:
var summary = from r in lf.AsQueryable<TelemetryDto>()
              group r by r.Location into g
              select new {
                  Location = g.Key,
                  AvgTemp = g.Average(x => x.Temperature)
              };
```

---

## 7. Polars.NET Exclusive: Strongly-Typed LINQ Merge (`TypedMerge`)

Polars.NET brings full **ANSI SQL `MERGE`** semantics directly into the C# and F# LINQ ecosystem:


```csharp [C# (TypedMerge)]
using Polars.CSharp;
using Polars.CSharp.Linq;

var targetQuery = targetDf.AsQueryable<ProductItem>();
var sourceQuery = sourceDf.AsQueryable<ProductItem>();

// Perform strongly-typed SQL MERGE using C# expression trees
using DataFrame resultDf = targetQuery.Merge(sourceQuery, t => t.Id, s => s.Id)
    // 1. Matched condition -> Delete
    .WhenMatched(
        (t, s) => s.IsDiscontinued,
        then => then.Delete()
    )
    // 2. Matched condition -> Update modified fields
    .WhenMatched(
        (t, s) => s.Price != t.Price,
        then => then.Update(set => set.Set(t => t.Price, (t, s) => s.Price))
    )
    // 3. Not matched in target -> Insert new item from source
    .WhenNotMatchedByTarget(
        s => s.Price > 0.0,
        then => then.Insert()
    )
    // 4. Not matched in source -> Delete obsolete target item
    .WhenNotMatchedBySource(
        t => t.Category == "Seasonal",
        then => then.Delete()
    )
    .ToDataFrame(); // Returns compiled DataFrame directly!
```

```fsharp [F# (Pipeline Merge)]
open Polars.FSharp

// F# functional pipeline merge
let mergedDf =
    targetDf.Merge(sourceDf, pl.col "Id")
    |> Merge.whenMatched (pl.col "IsDiscontinued") Merge.delete
    |> Merge.whenMatchedUpdateAll
    |> Merge.whenNotMatchedInsertAll
    |> Merge.executeEager
```


### Direct In-Memory Collection Merge (`List<T>.Merge(...)`)

The strongly-typed `Merge` builder can also be initiated directly on standard in-memory collections (`List<T>`, arrays, `IEnumerable<T>`), merging against another in-memory list or a Polars queryable:

```csharp
List<ProductItem> inMemoryTarget = GetTargetProducts();
List<ProductItem> incomingUpdates = GetSourceProducts();

// 1. Initiate full ANSI SQL MERGE directly from an in-memory List<T>:
using DataFrame mergedDf = inMemoryTarget.Merge(incomingUpdates, t => t.Id, s => s.Id)
    .WhenMatched(
        (t, s) => s.Price > t.Price,
        then => then.Update(set => set.Set(t => t.Price, (t, s) => s.Price))
    )
    .WhenNotMatchedByTarget(then => then.Insert())
    .WhenNotMatchedBySource(t => t.Category == "Seasonal", then => then.Delete())
    .ToDataFrame();

// 2. Or materialize directly back to typed entities:
List<ProductItem> updatedList = inMemoryTarget.Merge(incomingUpdates, t => t.Id, s => s.Id)
    .WhenMatched(then => then.Update(set => set.Set(t => t.Price, (t, s) => s.Price)))
    .WhenNotMatchedByTarget(then => then.Insert())
    .ToList();
```

# Chapter: Ecosystem Interoperability & Zero-Copy Bridges
*Source: articles/interop.md*

# Polars.NET Ecosystem Interoperability & Platform Runtimes

Polars.NET is designed as a foundational data engine for the .NET ecosystem. Beyond standalone dataframe queries, it provides zero-copy and streaming bridges to **Apache Arrow, ADBC, ADO.NET, ML.NET (IDataView), and modern .NET Tensors (`System.Numerics.Tensors`)**.

---

## 1. Native Runtime Packages (Different from Python!)

Unlike Python Polars (which distributes platform-specific self-contained wheels via `pip`), .NET NuGet separates managed API libraries from native binary packages to avoid package bloat.

### Required Package References
In any project using Polars.NET, you **must reference both**:
1. **The Managed API Library**: `Polars.CSharp` or `Polars.FSharp` (and optionally `Polars.NET.Linq`, `Polars.NET.ML`).
2. **The Native Runtime Package** matching your execution environment (OS and CPU Architecture):

```xml
<ItemGroup>
  <!-- 1. Managed API Library -->
  <PackageReference Include="Polars.CSharp" Version="1.0.0" />
  <PackageReference Include="Polars.NET.Linq" Version="1.0.0" />

  <!-- 2. Target Platform Native Binary (Pick according to your deployment OS/Arch) -->
  <!-- Windows x64: -->
  <PackageReference Include="Polars.NET.Native.win-x64" Version="1.0.0" Condition="$([MSBuild]::IsOSPlatform('Windows'))" />
  <!-- Linux x64 (glibc / Ubuntu / Debian / RHEL): -->
  <PackageReference Include="Polars.NET.Native.linux-x64" Version="1.0.0" Condition="$([MSBuild]::IsOSPlatform('Linux'))" />
  <!-- Linux ARM64: -->
  <!-- <PackageReference Include="Polars.NET.Native.linux-arm64" Version="1.0.0" /> -->
  <!-- Alpine Linux (musl): -->
  <!-- <PackageReference Include="Polars.NET.Native.linux-musl-x64" Version="1.0.0" /> -->
  <!-- macOS Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4): -->
  <PackageReference Include="Polars.NET.Native.osx-arm64" Version="1.0.0" Condition="$([MSBuild]::IsOSPlatform('OSX'))" />
</ItemGroup>
```

> [!IMPORTANT]
> If the native package is missing, you will receive `DllNotFoundException` for `libnative_shim.so`, `libnative_shim.dylib`, or `native_shim.dll` at runtime.

---

## 2. Managed Arrays, Spans & Collections

Polars.NET supports zero-copy span access for primitive numerics and fast hydration to/from standard .NET collections.

### Series to `ReadOnlySpan<T>` (Zero-Copy)
For contiguous numeric series (int, float, double, etc.), you can obtain a `ReadOnlySpan<T>` directly over native Arrow buffer memory without allocating a managed array:
```csharp
using var series = Series.From("temps", [20.5f, 21.0f, 22.3f]);

// Zero-copy span over native memory:
ReadOnlySpan<float> span = series.AsReadOnlySpan<float>();
float sum = 0f;
foreach (float val in span) { sum += val; }
```

### DataFrames to/from Rows & POCOs
```csharp
// 1. Ingest strongly-typed objects / records / List<T> into DataFrame (Most idiomatic .NET row pattern)
var records = new List<Order>
{
    new(1, "Widget", 19.99m),
    new(2, "Gadget", 49.50m)
};
using var df = DataFrame.FromRows(records);

// 2. Direct entry into the Polars native LINQ engine from any IEnumerable<T> / List<T>:
using Polars.CSharp.Linq;
using DataFrame topOrders = records.AsPolarsQueryable()
    .Where(o => o.Amount > 20.0m)
    .ToDataFrame();

// Seamlessly Join or Concat in-memory List<T> directly against a Polars query:
var extraOrders = new List<Order> { new(3, "Doohickey", 9.99m) };
using DataFrame allOrders = topOrders.AsQueryable<Order>()
    .Concat(extraOrders)
    .ToDataFrame();

// 3. Hydrate DataFrame back to strongly-typed sequence (or use LINQ)
IEnumerable<Order> orders = df.AsEnumerable<Order>();
```

---

## 3. Apache Arrow Integration (`Apache.Arrow`)

Polars columns are physically backed by Apache Arrow contiguous arrays. Polars.NET provides direct, zero-copy interoperability with the official `Apache.Arrow` .NET package.

### Zero-Copy `RecordBatch` Ingestion & Export


```csharp [C# (Arrow RecordBatch)]
using Apache.Arrow;
using Apache.Arrow.Memory;
using Polars.CSharp;

// 1. Build or receive a native Apache.Arrow RecordBatch:
var allocator = new NativeMemoryAllocator();
var batch = new RecordBatch.Builder(allocator)
    .Append("SensorId", false, col => col.Int32(arr => arr.AppendRange([101, 102, 103])))
    .Append("Temperature", false, col => col.Double(arr => arr.AppendRange([24.5, 26.1, 23.8])))
    .Build();

// 2. Zero-Copy import into Polars DataFrame:
using var df = DataFrame.FromArrow(batch);

// 3. Roundtrip back to Apache.Arrow RecordBatch:
using RecordBatch exportedBatch = df.ToArrow();
```

```fsharp [F# (Arrow RecordBatch)]
open Apache.Arrow
open Apache.Arrow.Memory
open Polars.FSharp

// Zero-copy ingestion from Apache.Arrow RecordBatch:
let df = DataFrame.FromArrow(batch)

// Roundtrip back to Apache.Arrow RecordBatch:
use exportedBatch = df.ToArrow()
```




### Arrow-to-Arrow Vectorized UDFs
When implementing advanced custom vector processing, use `MapArrow` to bypass row-by-row boxing and process raw `Apache.Arrow.IArrowArray`:

```csharp
var customExpr = Pl.Col("features").MapArrow(
    arrowArray => MyCustomArrowKernel(arrowArray),
    outputType: DataType.Float64
);
```

---

## 4. ADBC (Arrow Database Connectivity)

[ADBC](https://arrow.apache.org/adbc/) is the next-generation database standard that transfers tabular data as binary Apache Arrow record batches, eliminating slow row-by-row ODBC/JDBC serialization.

Polars.NET includes built-in first-class ADBC support for DuckDB, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Snowflake, and BigQuery via `Apache.Arrow.Adbc`:

```csharp
using Apache.Arrow.Adbc;

// 1. Query an ADBC database directly into a zero-copy DataFrame
using var df = DataFrame.ReadAdbc(adbcConnection, "SELECT id, amount, customer FROM orders WHERE amount > 100");

// 2. Zero-Copy Bulk Ingest a DataFrame into an ADBC Database
// Ingest modes: AdbcIngestMode.Create, AdbcIngestMode.Append, AdbcIngestMode.Replace
var updateResult = df.WriteToAdbc(adbcConnection, "target_table", AdbcIngestMode.Append);
Console.WriteLine($"Inserted {updateResult.AffectedRows} rows");
```

---

## 5. ADO.NET (`System.Data`)

For traditional relational databases (SQL Server, Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL via Npgsql, SQLite via Microsoft.Data.Sqlite), Polars.NET integrates directly with `IDataReader` and `DbDataReader`.

### Reading Database Queries into DataFrames (`ReadDatabase` / `ReadDb`)

`DataFrame.ReadDatabase` accepts any open `IDataReader` and converts rows directly into Arrow record batches with prefetching:


```csharp [C# (ReadDatabase)]
using System.Data;
using Microsoft.Data.SqlClient; // Or Npgsql, SqliteConnection, etc.
using Polars.CSharp;

using var connection = new SqlConnection(connectionString);
connection.Open();

using var command = connection.CreateCommand();
command.CommandText = "SELECT Product, Price, CreatedAt FROM Sales WHERE Price > 100";

using IDataReader reader = command.ExecuteReader();

// Streams from IDataReader into Arrow batches -> Materialized Polars DataFrame:
using DataFrame df = DataFrame.ReadDatabase(reader, batchSize: 50_000);
```

```fsharp [F# (ReadDb)]
open System.Data
open Microsoft.Data.SqlClient
open Polars.FSharp

use connection = new SqlConnection(connectionString)
connection.Open()

use command = connection.CreateCommand()
command.CommandText <- "SELECT Product, Price, CreatedAt FROM Sales WHERE Price > 100"

use reader = command.ExecuteReader()

// Stream into Polars DataFrame
use df = DataFrame.ReadDb(reader, batchSize = 50_000)
```


> [!NOTE] Automatic Data Type Mappings
> `ReadDatabase` automatically maps standard ADO.NET types to their native Polars equivalents:
> * `decimal` -> Polars `Decimal128` (arbitrary precision without rounding loss)
> * `DateTime` / `DateOnly` / `TimeOnly` -> Polars `Datetime` / `Date` / `Time`
> * `Guid` / `string` -> Polars `String`
> * `DBNull.Value` -> Polars nulls

---

### Lazy Database Scanning (`LazyFrame.ScanDatabase` / `ScanDb`)

For pipeline queries, prefer `LazyFrame.ScanDatabase`. It supports passing either an existing `IDataReader` or a **reader factory** `Func<IDataReader>`. 

> [!TIP] Why Use a Reader Factory?
> A factory allows Polars to probe schema upfront with a quick probe query and re-execute queries if the query plan requires multiple execution passes or reuse:


```csharp [C# (Lazy Scan with Reader Factory)]
using System.Data;
using Polars.CSharp;

// Define a factory that returns a fresh open IDataReader on demand:
Func<IDataReader> readerFactory = () =>
{
    var cmd = connection.CreateCommand();
    cmd.CommandText = "SELECT Name, Score, Dept FROM Employees WHERE Score >= 60.0";
    return cmd.ExecuteReader();
};

using LazyFrame lf = LazyFrame.ScanDatabase(readerFactory, batchSize: 50_000);

using DataFrame result = lf
    .Filter(Pl.Col("Dept") == "Engineering")
    .GroupBy("Dept")
    .Agg(Pl.Col("Score").Mean().Alias("AvgScore"))
    .Collect();
```

```fsharp [F# (Lazy Scan with Reader Factory)]
open System.Data
open Polars.FSharp

let readerFactory () =
    let cmd = connection.CreateCommand()
    cmd.CommandText <- "SELECT Name, Score, Dept FROM Employees WHERE Score >= 60.0"
    cmd.ExecuteReader() :> IDataReader

use lf = LazyFrame.ScanDb(readerFactory, batchSize = 50_000)

use result =
    lf
    |> LazyFrame.filter (pl.col "Dept" .== pl.lit "Engineering")
    |> LazyFrame.groupBy [ pl.col "Dept" ]
    |> LazyFrame.agg [ pl.col("Score").Mean().Alias "AvgScore" ]
    |> LazyFrame.collect
```


---

### Direct LINQ Pipeline Entrypoint (`reader.AsPolarsQueryable<T>`)

Instead of materializing an intermediate `DataFrame`, you can stream an open `IDataReader` directly into a Polars LINQ queryable pipeline with native Rust plan compilation:

```csharp
using System.Data;
using Polars.CSharp;
using Polars.CSharp.Linq;

using IDataReader reader = command.ExecuteReader();

// Streams database cursor directly into Polars LINQ engine:
using DataFrame summaryDf = reader.AsPolarsQueryable<SaleDto>(batchSize: 50_000)
    .Where(s => s.Price > 100.0)
    .GroupBy(s => s.Product)
    .Select(g => new { Product = g.Key, TotalRevenue = g.Sum(x => x.Price) })
    .ToDataFrame();
```

---

### Asynchronous Chunk Streaming (`ReadDatabaseBatchesAsync`)

When dealing with large query results, use `DbDataReader.ReadDatabaseBatchesAsync` to stream materialized DataFrame batches asynchronously without blocking the thread pool:


```csharp [C# (Async Batch Ingestion)]
using System.Data.Common;
using Polars.CSharp;

using DbDataReader reader = await command.ExecuteReaderAsync();

// Stream database cursor records into chunks of native Polars DataFrames:
await foreach (DataFrame batch in reader.ReadDatabaseBatchesAsync(batchSize: 50_000))
{
    using (batch)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Ingested {batch.Height} rows.");
        // Process each batch or push to downstream worker
    }
}
```

```fsharp [F# (Async Batch Ingestion)]
open Polars.FSharp

task {
    use! reader = command.ExecuteReaderAsync()
    for batch in reader.ReadDatabaseBatchesAsync(batchSize = 50_000) do
        use b = batch
        printfn $"Ingested %d{b.Height} rows."
}
```


---

### Direct LINQ Pipeline Entrypoint (`reader.AsPolarsQueryable<T>`)

Instead of materializing an intermediate `DataFrame`, you can stream an open `IDataReader` directly into a Polars LINQ queryable pipeline with native Rust plan compilation:

```csharp
using System.Data;
using Polars.CSharp;
using Polars.CSharp.Linq;

using IDataReader reader = command.ExecuteReader();

// Streams database cursor directly into Polars LINQ engine:
using DataFrame summaryDf = reader.AsPolarsQueryable<SaleDto>(batchSize: 50_000)
    .Where(s => s.Price > 100.0)
    .GroupBy(s => s.Product)
    .Select(g => new { Product = g.Key, TotalRevenue = g.Sum(x => x.Price) })
    .ToDataFrame();
```

---

### Exporting & Writing to Databases (`WriteTo`, `SinkTo`, `AsDataReader`)

To write Polars DataFrames into database tables (such as bulk insertion with `SqlBulkCopy`), Polars.NET provides two zero-memory-copy producer-consumer patterns:

#### Pattern 1: `df.WriteTo(Action<IDataReader>)` & `lf.SinkTo(Action<IDataReader>)`
`WriteTo` streams Arrow batches into an internal bounded queue and provides an active `IDataReader` to your writer callback:


```csharp [C# (SqlBulkCopy with WriteTo)]
using System.Data;
using Microsoft.Data.SqlClient;
using Polars.CSharp;

// Stream rows directly from Polars DataFrame into SQL Server SqlBulkCopy:
df.WriteTo(reader =>
{
    using var bulkCopy = new SqlBulkCopy(connectionString);
    bulkCopy.DestinationTableName = "dbo.TargetSales";
    bulkCopy.BatchSize = 10_000;
    bulkCopy.WriteToServer(reader);
}, bufferSize: 5);
```

```fsharp [F# (SqlBulkCopy with WriteTo)]
open System
open System.Data
open Microsoft.Data.SqlClient
open Polars.FSharp

df.WriteTo(
    Action<IDataReader>(fun reader ->
        use bulkCopy = new SqlBulkCopy(connectionString)
        bulkCopy.DestinationTableName <- "dbo.TargetSales"
        bulkCopy.BatchSize <- 10_000
        bulkCopy.WriteToServer reader
    ),
    bufferSize = 5
)
```


#### Pattern 2: `df.AsDataReader()` (Zero-Copy `DbDataReader`)
Alternatively, obtain a live `DbDataReader` instance directly using `df.AsDataReader()`:

```csharp
using System.Data.Common;
using Microsoft.Data.SqlClient;

// Obtain a live DbDataReader backed by a Polars bounded channel:
using DbDataReader reader = df.AsDataReader(bufferSize: 5);

using var bulkCopy = new SqlBulkCopy(connectionString);
bulkCopy.DestinationTableName = "dbo.TargetSales";
bulkCopy.WriteToServer(reader);
```

---

## 6. Machine Learning: Microsoft.ML / ML.NET (`IDataView`)

Through the `Polars.NET.ML` package, Polars.NET bridges Polars DataFrames with ML.NET's `IDataView` pipeline.

```csharp
using Microsoft.ML;
using Polars.NET.ML.DataView;
using Polars.NET.ML.CSharpExtensions;

var mlContext = new MLContext();

// 1. Convert Polars DataFrame to ML.NET IDataView (Zero-copy stream)
IDataView dataView = df.AsDataView();

// 2. Train an ML.NET pipeline directly on Polars data
var pipeline = mlContext.Transforms.NormalizeMinMax("Features")
    .Append(mlContext.Regression.Trainers.Sdca(labelColumnName: "Target", featureColumnName: "Features"));
var model = pipeline.Fit(dataView);

// 3. Transform predictions back to a Polars DataFrame
IDataView predictions = model.Transform(dataView);
using DataFrame resultDf = predictions.ToDataFrame();
```

---

## 7. AI & Deep Learning: Tensors (`System.Numerics.Tensors`)

Modern .NET 8 / 9+ includes `System.Numerics.Tensors.Tensor<T>` and `ReadOnlyTensorSpan<T>`. Polars.NET provides direct, native conversions for feeding models in **ONNX Runtime, TorchSharp, or native C++ inference engines**.

### Series to Tensor / TensorSpan
```csharp
using System.Numerics.Tensors;

using var embSeries = df["embeddings"]; // e.g. Array[f32, 128] or flat Series

// 1. Zero-copy TensorSpan view
ReadOnlyTensorSpan<float> tensorSpan = embSeries.AsTensorSpan<float>();

// 2. Transposed view without moving bytes (zero-copy stride transposition)
ReadOnlyTensorSpan<float> transposed = embSeries.AsTransposedTensorSpan<float>();

// 3. Deep-copy into managed heap Tensor<T> (safe for async/background tasks)
Tensor<float> managedTensor = embSeries.AsTensor<float>();
```

### DataFrame to 2D Feature Matrix Tensor
Extract selected columns and format them into a 2D Row-Major `Tensor<T> [Rows, Columns]`:
```csharp
// Extracts "age", "income", "credit_score" into a 2D [N, 3] row-major tensor for ONNX
Tensor<float> featureMatrix = df.AsTensor<float>("age", "income", "credit_score");
```

### Raw Unmanaged Memory Pointer (Zero-Copy C++ / ONNX FFI)
```csharp
// Direct pointer to contiguous Arrow memory for native C++ backends
(nint ptr, long[] shape) = series.AsDangerousUnmanagedTensor<float>();

try
{
    CallNativeCppInferenceEngine(ptr, shape);
}
finally
{
    // Prevent GC from collecting Series while native engine reads the pointer
    GC.KeepAlive(series);
}
```

---

## 8. Asynchronous Streaming (`IAsyncEnumerable`)

Polars.NET provides first-class support for C# `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` and F# async row streams, enabling cooperative, cancellation-aware asynchronous processing without thread pool starvation.

### C# Row Streaming (`ToAsyncEnumerable`)
```csharp
using Polars.CSharp;

using var df = DataFrame.ReadParquet("large.parquet");

// Stream rows cooperatively (yields execution slots to avoid starving thread pool)
await foreach (var row in df.ToAsyncEnumerable<MyRecord>(chunkSize: 10_000, cancellationToken))
{
    await ProcessRowAsync(row);
}
```

### Lazy Native Batch Streaming (`CollectBatchesAsync`)

Stream materialized DataFrame chunks from a `LazyFrame` as soon as they are computed by the native Rust streaming engine:


```csharp [C# (Async Batch Streaming)]
using Polars.CSharp;

using var lf = LazyFrame.ScanParquet("huge_dataset/*.parquet");

// Asynchronously stream DataFrame batches:
await foreach (DataFrame batch in lf.CollectBatchesAsync(chunkSize: 50_000))
{
    using (batch)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Received streaming batch of {batch.Height} rows");
        await ExportBatchToCloudAsync(batch);
    }
}
```

```fsharp [F# (Async Batch Streaming)]
open Polars.FSharp

let lf = LazyFrame.ScanParquet "huge_dataset/*.parquet"

task {
    for batch in lf.CollectBatchesAsync(chunkSize = 50_000L) do
        use b = batch
        printfn $"Received streaming batch of %d{b.Height} rows"
        do! exportBatchToCloud b
}
```


### LINQ & `IAsyncEnumerable` Adaptation
```csharp
using Polars.CSharp.Linq;

// 1. Convert LINQ query directly to IAsyncEnumerable:
IAsyncEnumerable<OrderDto> asyncStream = query.AsAsyncEnumerable();

// 2. Ingest foreign IAsyncEnumerable into a Polars DataFrame asynchronously:
IAsyncEnumerable<SensorData> externalStream = FetchDataFromGrpcAsync();
using DataFrame df = await externalStream.ToDataFrameAsync(cancellationToken);
```

### F# Async Row Streams (`RowsAsync`)
```fsharp
open Polars.FSharp

// Stream rows into F# list/array or functional pipeline:
let! records =
    df.RowsAsync<SensorRecord>(chunkSize = 5000)
    |> RowsAsync.filter (fun s -> s.Temperature > 25.0)
    |> RowsAsync.toList

// Aggregate over async stream without materializing entire dataset:
let! totalTemp =
    lazyDf.RowsAsync<SensorRecord>(chunkSize = 10000L, engine = Engine.Auto)
    |> RowsAsync.fold (fun acc s -> acc + s.Temperature) 0.0
```

---
